lines: The safehouse was a single dim room over a shuttered shop — a cot, a sink, a first-aid kit she'd stashed there years ago for exactly this kind of night.

You got her onto the cot under the bare bulb. The wound was worse than a graze and better than your worst fear: the round had carved a deep line along her ribs, ugly and bleeding but survivable, if you cleaned it and closed it now.

She talked you through it in a tight, steady voice — antiseptic, needle, the stitches she couldn't reach herself — and you worked over her side with hands you kept very still, because the alternative was letting them shake.
She watched your face the whole time. Not the wound. Your face.
It was a strange kind of intimacy — quieter and more naked than any of the gala's performances.

No cover here. No mic in the corner, no audience to sell anything to. Just a wounded woman trusting a man with a needle near her ribs, and a man trying not to let her see how badly the sight of her hurt had rattled him.
When you tied off the last stitch and pressed the bandage flat, she let out a breath she'd been holding for an hour and let her head fall back against the wall.
And then, in the low yellow light, with her guard finally, fully gone, she said the thing she'd been circling all week.
When that shot hit me, you know what scared me? It wasn't dying. I made peace with dying a long time ago.
It was the look on your face. For half a second I saw you decide you'd rather take the next one than watch me go down again. And I thought — oh no. Oh, this is real. This is the thing I don't do.
I've spent fifteen years making sure no one would ever make that face about me. Because that face gets people killed. That face is a liability.
And I'm lying here bleeding in my own safehouse desperately glad you made it anyway. So tell me, gently, because I'm out of armor tonight — what are we doing? 🩹
She lay back against the wall, bandaged, undefended, looking up at you with the last of her walls down.
What do you tell her?

choices.label: I made that face because somewhere this week you stopped being my cover and started being the person I can't lose.
We're doing the thing neither of us is supposed to do. And I'm done pretending I'm not all the way in.
(You brush the hair from her face — the gesture from the plane, no cover left in it now — and hold her eyes.)
choices.me: You brush the hair from her face — the same gesture as the plane, but with nothing left to hide behind — and hold her eyes.

lines: …The person you can't lose. 🥺
Do you understand what you're handing me? I could use that. The old me would file it under 'leverage' and walk away clean.
Instead I'm lying here wanting to be that for you so badly it terrifies me more than the bullet did.
You've ruined fifteen years of very careful work in five days, husband. …I'm not even angry. That's the worst part. 🩹
All the way in. 😶
You say it like it's simple. Like people like us get to just be all the way in on something.
…But you said it without flinching, with my blood still on your hands, and I believe you. God help me, I believe you.
Then I'm in too. There. It's out. Two of the most careful people alive, both all the way in, and not a single one of us has a plan for it. 🩹
That's the plane. The hair thing. You did it on the jet to learn the cover and I told myself it meant nothing.
There's no cover now. No cameras. Nobody to sell it to. And you did it anyway.
…So it was never the cover. Not for you. Maybe not for me either. …Don't move your hand. Leave it right there. 🩹
You stayed close in the dim room while the adrenaline drained out of you both and the long night settled.

She didn't pull back into the cold operator. For once she let herself be tended — let you bring her water, fix her bandage, sit with your back against the cot as she lay there too wired and too wrung-out to sleep.
Her hand found yours in the dark and held it. Not tactical. Not cover. Just held it, the way a person holds onto a thing they've decided they want.
You were close enough to cross the last inch. You both knew it. And tonight, finally, neither of you was looking for a reason not to.
Not tonight, though. Not like this — me half-stitched and shaking and high on the fact that I'm not dead.
When it happens — and it's going to, we both feel it — I want to be all the way here for it. Not bleeding. Not running. Just us.
There's one loose end first. The tap only caught half of what we need; my contact says Volkov's lieutenant carries the rest on him. We finish the job clean, then we finish… this.
Sleep, husband. Hold my hand and keep watch like you do. Tomorrow we go back to work. 🩹
(To be continued — Chapter 10: Honeypot 🍸)
